# Second World War dates — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/world-war-ii.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/world-war-ii.ttl`](../decks/world-war-ii.ttl) · **Cards:** 47 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

47 key events of the Second World War, from the Marco Polo Bridge incident in 1937 to Japan's surrender on 2 September 1945, spread across Europe, the Nordic countries, the Atlantic, North Africa, Asia and the Pacific. The front describes the event in English and Swedish; the back gives its date as day, month and year, e.g. “1 September 1939”. Only events with an undisputed single-day date are included, such as the start of a battle, a declaration of war, a signature or a surrender. Dates from Wikidata, checked against Store norske leksikon, the Imperial War Museums, the US Office of the Historian and Liberation Route Europe.

## Licensing

The only content source is Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0: the dates and the Swedish and English names of events, ships and places used on the cards come from it, so the deck is CC0 1.0 like the rest of the library. Store norske leksikon (articles marked begrenset gjenbruk, all rights reserved, and a few marked CC BY-SA 3.0), the Imperial War Museums and Liberation Route Europe (all rights reserved) and the US Department of State's Office of the Historian (a US government work, not under copyright in the US) were used for verification only: they confirmed dates that Wikidata gave, and short quotations of them appear only in the provenance report as evidence. No table or selection was copied from them, and no wording beyond bare factual statements: some fronts resemble rows of SNL's timeline (for example "The Norwegian forces in Norway capitulate" and the row "De gjenværende norske styrkene i Norge kapitulerer") because both state the same bare fact in the usual way, and such minimal factual statements are not protected expression; the selection of events was made by the authoring agent from general knowledge before any of them was consulted. The fronts and notes are the compiler's own wording of facts. Added after the first review round, for verification only as well: the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia (all rights reserved) and English and Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0); from Swedish Wikipedia only the bare Swedish names "Dagen D", "andra slaget vid el-Alamein" and "mellanfreden i Moskva" were confirmed, which are not protected expression, so the deck stays CC0.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a script extracting dated sentences from Store norske leksikon, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. Candidates: from its own general knowledge, the authoring agent drew up 118 search strings for widely taught events of the Second World War, deliberately covering every theatre (Europe, the Nordic countries, the Atlantic, the Mediterranean and North Africa, China, South-East Asia and the Pacific) and including the Holocaust. No published list or timeline was copied. Each string was looked up with the Wikidata wbsearchentities API (queries 1 and 2, script <scratch>/search.py) and the item for the event picked by hand from the hits and their descriptions.
3. Dates and labels: one SPARQL query (query 3) returned, for about 100 candidate items, their English and Swedish labels and every P585 point in time, P580 start time, P582 end time, P571 inception and P576 dissolution date with its precision and rank. The raw CSV was saved and read item by item (script <scratch>/show.py). Only day-precision values (precision 11) of normal or preferred rank were used; a deprecated value (Victory in Europe Day's P585) was not.
4. Choosing the event and its date: for each card the moment named on the front is exactly the one Wikidata dates: the start (P580) of an invasion, battle or operation, the end (P582) where the front names a surrender or the end of an evacuation, and the point in time (P585) of a signature, declaration, conference or bombing. Where one item's dates could be read two ways the front was worded to name the moment that the date belongs to (the last German troops at Stalingrad, the German garrison of Paris, Italy's secret signature at Cassibile, the signature of the Moscow Armistice). The machine checks compare the full date ("1939-09-01T00:00:00Z"), not only the year, against live Wikidata.
5. Independent check: every card's date was checked against at least one authority independent of Wikidata. For most cards this is Store norske leksikon (SNL), the Norwegian national encyclopedia whose articles are written by named subject experts: for each card the SNL search API (https://snl.no/api/v1/search) was queried with one to four Norwegian search strings (queries 4, 5 and 7), the article JSON of the top hits fetched (https://snl.no/<article>.json) and the sentences that contain the card's day and month in Norwegian form ("1. september") together with its year extracted by the script <scratch>/snl.py. SNL's chronological table "andre verdenskrig – viktige hendelser" turned up among the hits and was read row by row. Where SNL gave no date for the event, the Imperial War Museums (El Alamein, Tunisia, Okinawa), the US Department of State's Office of the Historian (Marco Polo Bridge, also Tripartite Pact and Pearl Harbor) and Liberation Route Europe (Cassibile, Paris) were consulted (query 8; pages saved with curl and their sentences extracted with <scratch>/grep.py). The verbatim sentence or table row is in each card's evidence, Norwegian quotes with an English gloss in brackets. The US National WWII Museum's timeline was also tried: its URL answered 404 and it was not used; the US Army Center of Military History answered 403 and the US Naval History and Heritage Command failed certificate verification (both listed under query 8), so neither was used. After the first review round, the Axis surrender in Tunisia was also checked against the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia, the Continuation War's start and the Okinawa landings against English Wikipedia, and the Swedish names "Dagen D", "andra slaget vid el-Alamein" and "mellanfreden i Moskva" against Swedish Wikipedia (query 11; all verification only).
6. Swedish text: every front is the deck's own wording of the event in English and in Swedish, written by the authoring agent in Swedish conventions (sentence case, lower-case month names on the back: "1 september 1939"). Swedish names of events, places and ships were taken from Wikidata's sv labels (queries 3 and 6): vinterkriget, Moskvafreden, Operation Weserübung, Operation Dynamo, Dunkerque, Blitzen, Operation Barbarossa, Belägringen av Leningrad, Wannseekonferensen, Slaget vid Río de la Plata, Admiral Graf Spee, Bismarck, Operation Torch, Upproret i Warszawas getto, Slaget vid Kursk, Warszawaupproret, Ardenneroffensiven, Jaltakonferensen, Marco Polo-broincidenten, Molotov–Ribbentrop-pakten, Mellanfreden i Moskva, fortsättningskriget; each one used on a front has a label check ("mellanfreden i Moskva" is written in lower case in running text, as Swedish writes the names of treaties, and "Fortsättningskriget" is capitalised only because it opens the sentence). Other names follow the sv labels of the places (Warszawa, Normandie, Jugoslavien, Grekland, Tunisien, Storbritannien, Sovjetunionen) and the Swedish label of Victory in Europe Day (Q622365, "Segerdagen i Europa"; Swedish writes the names of holidays in lower case, and "Segerdagen" is capitalised in the Reims card's note only because it opens the sentence). "el-Alamein" follows the sv label of the battle item (Q153376, "Slaget vid el-Alamein"); "Andra slaget vid el-Alamein" follows Swedish Wikipedia ("Slaget vid el-Alamein, eller mer korrekt andra slaget vid el-Alamein"), and "Dagen D" is the established Swedish name for 6 June 1944 per Swedish Wikipedia ("Landstigningarna inleddes tisdagen den 6 juni 1944 (Dagen D)"). Pact names that are common nouns in Swedish running text are written in lower case ("tremaktspakten"), so they carry no label check.
7. Back convention: the date is written out as day, month name and year in each language ("1 September 1939" / "1 september 1939"), the form used in both English and Swedish reference works. Dates are the local dates of the place where the event happened, as Wikidata and the checking sources give them.
8. Notes: a backNote is added only where a related date is easily confused with the card's (the main surrender at Stalingrad on 31 January, the Winter War fighting ending on 13 March, the announcement of the Italian armistice on 8 September, VE Day on 8 May, the start of the Dunkirk evacuation) or gives brief context; every note's content is in the card's evidence.
9. Build and validation: the dossier JSON was generated from the saved query results by <scratch>/make_dossier.py (the Wikidata evidence texts are generated from the query 3 CSV; the other evidence texts were copied from the script output into <scratch>/cards.py), built with python3 packages/deck-library/scripts/authored_decks.py build world-war-ii, which re-ran every Wikidata check (the full date of every card and the labels used) against live Wikidata, and validated with node packages/deck-library/scripts/validate_sources.ts world-war-ii (the app's SHACL shapes and DCAT-AP).

## Selection

Included: 47 widely taught events of the Second World War whose date is a single day that Wikidata and an independent authority agree on: the start of an invasion, battle or operation, a declaration of war, the signature of a pact, armistice or surrender, a conference's opening, a bombing, a landing. The set covers the war's whole span (from the Marco Polo Bridge incident of 7 July 1937, which began the war between Japan and China, to Japan's signature of surrender on 2 September 1945) and all theatres: Europe (including the Holocaust), the Nordic countries (the Winter War, the Moscow Peace Treaty, Operation Weserübung, Norway's capitulation, the Continuation War, the Moscow Armistice), the Atlantic (the River Plate, the Bismarck), North Africa (El Alamein, Operation Torch, the surrender in Tunisia) and Asia and the Pacific. Left out because the sources give different dates or the start of the event is defined differently: the Battle of Midway (Wikidata 4–7 June, SNL 3–6 June 1942), the Battle of Britain (Wikidata from 10 July, SNL from 10 August 1940), the Atlantic Charter (Wikidata 14 August, SNL 12 August 1941), the Allied invasion of Sicily (Wikidata 9 July, SNL 10 July 1943), the Battle of Iwo Jima (Wikidata's start is 8 February 1945, while the authoring agent knew the main landings to be usually dated 19 February; left out without further research), the Lapland War, the Battle of the Coral Sea, the Battle of Leyte Gulf and the Battle of Berlin (left out without further research because, to the authoring agent's knowledge, accounts define their start differently), the Liberation of Paris as a whole (SNL dates it 24 August; the card is instead the garrison's surrender on 25 August), Victory in Europe Day as a card of its own (its Wikidata date is deprecated; it is in the note of the Reims card), Italy's declaration of war on France and Britain (the only Wikidata item found was the Italian invasion of France, a different event), the Lend-Lease Act and the British occupation of Iceland (no date in Wikidata). Further candidates (among them Mers-el-Kébir, Taranto, the Tehran Conference, Operation Bagration, the fall of Hong Kong, the bombing of Darwin, the Doolittle Raid, the Potsdam Declaration and the Hirohito broadcast) were left out only to keep the deck at about 45 cards and balanced between theatres. The deck stops at 2 September 1945; nothing in it depends on events after that date.

## Quality control

7 rounds, 35 findings: 28 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 6 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (93 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks: every card's date against Wikidata (full date, day precision) and against an independent authority (Store norske leksikon, the Imperial War Museums, the US Office of the Historian or Liberation Route Europe); the Swedish names against Wikidata sv labels. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 47 cards, the candidates left out, the sources and the deck metadata.

For all 47 cards Wikidata's date and the independent source agree on the day of the moment named on the front. Where sources differed on a related moment (the main versus the final surrender at Stalingrad, the entry of French troops into Paris versus the German surrender, the Italian armistice's signature versus its announcement, the signature versus the effect of the Moscow treaties, Reims versus VE Day) the front names the moment and a note gives the other date. Candidates whose dates differ between the sources were left out. No Wikidata check was skipped.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| battle-of-midway | Wikidata dates the Battle of Midway 4–7 June 1942 (P580/P582); SNL's chronology gives "3.–6. juni". | Left out: the start date depends on what counts as the start of the battle. | fixed |
| stalingrad-surrender | Wikidata's end of the Battle of Stalingrad is 2 February 1943; SNL's chronology lists "31. januar \| Tysk kapitulasjon i Stalingrad". Both are right: the main German force surrendered on 31 January, the last units on 2 February (SNL "Østfronten"). | Front "The last German troops at Stalingrad surrender", back 2 February 1943, note on 31 January. | fixed |
| liberation-of-paris | Wikidata's end of the Liberation of Paris is 25 August 1944; SNL's chronology gives "24. august \| Paris befris". Liberation Route Europe: French troops reached the centre on the evening of 24 August; on 25 August the capitulation was signed. | Front names the German garrison's surrender (25 August); note on the evening of 24 August. | fixed |
| moscow-peace-treaty | SNL's chronology gives "12.–13. mars" for the peace; Wikidata dates the treaty 12 March (P585) and the end of the Winter War 13 March (P582). | Front says the treaty was signed (12 March); note that the fighting stopped on 13 March. | fixed |
| moscow-armistice | SNL's chronology dates the ceasefire 4 September 1944 and notes it was signed on 19 September; Wikidata's Moscow Armistice is 19 September (P585), as is the end of the Continuation War (P582). | Front names the signature (19 September); note that a ceasefire had held since early September. | fixed |
| germany-surrenders-at-reims | Wikidata's German Instrument of Surrender (Q700983) has both P585 7 May and P580 8 May 1945; Victory in Europe Day's P585 (8 May) is deprecated, so a check on it would fail. | The card is the signature at Reims, dated by the item "Preliminary surrender document in Reims" (Q20872997, P585 7 May 1945) and confirmed by SNL; the note gives VE Day, 8 May, checked against Q700983 P580. | fixed |
| armistice-of-cassibile | The armistice was signed on 3 September 1943 but made public on 8 September; SNL's chronology lists only the announcement ("8. september \| Italiensk kunngjøring om våpenhvile"). | Front says Italy secretly signs at Cassibile; Liberation Route Europe confirms 3 September; note on 8 September. | fixed |
| dunkirk-evacuation-ends | Wikidata's description of the Dunkirk evacuation says "between 27 May and 4 June 1940" while its P580 is 26 May (SNL: 26 May to 4 June). | The card asks for the end (4 June), on which all sources agree; the note names 26 May as Wikidata's and SNL's start. | fixed |
| siege-of-leningrad-begins | SNL's article on Lidija Ginzburg dates the siege 8 September 1941 – 17 January 1944; Wikidata's end is 27 January 1944. | The card uses only the start (8 September 1941), on which they agree; the end is not on any card. | no change needed |
| bismarck-sunk | The SNL sentence spells the cruiser "HMS Dorshetshire" (HMS Dorsetshire). | Quoted verbatim; the gloss gives the usual spelling. The card does not name the cruiser. | no change needed |
| continuation-war-begins | SNL says that on 25 June 1941 the Finnish army crossed the eastern border; the war's start date is 25 June in both Wikidata and SNL's chronology ("Finland i krig med Sovjetunionen"). | Front says only that the war begins; the note (three days after Germany's attack on 22 June) is in the SNL sentence. | no change needed |
| axis-surrender-in-tunisia | The Wikidata item that dates the end (Q111976845, "Tunisia Campaign", a US Army campaign) has no Swedish label; no SNL article stating 13 May 1943 was found (one search timed out). | Date checked against the Imperial War Museums ("The North Africa Campaign was fought from 10 June 1940 to 13 May 1943."); Swedish wording is the deck's own. | no change needed |
| germany-invades-poland | Wikidata's description of the invasion says it "marked the start of World War II", while SNL (Edward Wood Halifax) calls the British declaration of 3 September "starten på andre verdenskrig". | No card or note claims which event began the war. | no change needed |

### Round 1: Factual accuracy (2026-10-04)
